item.title: BE ALERT - YELLOW WARNING - RAINFALL - IN EFFECT
item.description:
Generic Warning | Yellow Warning - Rainfall - In Effect |

Heavy rain will continue today. A low pressure system is bringing heavy rain to northern Manitoba. By the time rain becomes light this afternoon, a total of 25 to 40 mm is expected. Light rain will continue until Saturday afternoon. Parks and forests will likely sustain some damage. Landslides may occur in vulnerable areas such as steep slopes, deforested areas or recent burn scars. Rainfall warnings are issued when significant impacts are expected due to rainfall amounts. Please continue to monitor alerts and forecasts issued by Environment Canada. To report severe weather, send an email to MBstorm@ec.gc.ca, call 1-800-239-0484 or post reports on social media using MBStorm.

item.title: 2027 Envirothon - Current Environmental Topic
item.description:
2027 Envirothon - Current Environmental Topic kfarrar Thu, 09/10/2026 - 14:41

Maryland, host of the 2027 NCF-Envirothon international competition, has chosen the theme "Soil Health Management: Agricultural Principles and Stewardship" as its Current Environmental Issue (CEI). 

Please see the synopsis below regarding the CEI:

Soil Health Principles emphasize the importance of treating soil as a living ecosystem and are the cornerstone for resilient agriculture and ensuring the long-term protection of our natural resources. Maryland has become a national leader in soil health stewardship driven by its commitment to sustainable agriculture and Chesapeake Bay restoration. Farmers from across Maryland have integrated these principles with nutrient management and conservation strategies, making it a model for climate-smart farming. Maryland’s agricultural sector plays a vital role in protecting the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries through the adoption of soil health practices.

Maryland’s Cover Crop Program is recognized as one of the most successful in the United States. Each year, Maryland farmers plant over 450,000 acres of cover crops, which helps reduce soil erosion, improve soil organic matter, and capture residual nutrients before they leach into waterways. Maryland Farmers also embraced conservation tillage and no-till farming, with more than 50% of cropland managed under reduced tillage systems. These practices protect soil structure, enhance microbial activity, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Such efforts demonstrate how healthy soils not only sustain crop productivity but also serve as a powerful tool for water quality improvement and ecosystem restoration. Farmers and conservation professionals are using soil health principles to restore degraded soils and reduce pollution. In Maryland, these efforts have directly improved the Chesapeake Bay’s water quality through reduced nutrient runoff, increased infiltration, and better soil structure. The insights gained from Maryland farmers can be applied worldwide to help promote sustainability in agricultural practices.

This Envirothon issue explores the biological, chemical, and physical principles of soil health and their importance to sustainable agriculture. Students will learn how soil functions as a living ecosystem, how management practices affect soil processes (nutrient cycling, water dynamics, agricultural sustainability), and how to evaluate and improve soil health on farms.

item.title: New funding available through Anti-Racism Grants
item.description:
New funding available through Anti-Racism Grants jenniferdhogan Thu, 09/10/2026 - 14:20

Applications are open for the 2026-2027 Anti-Racism Grants with a total of $275,000 in funding available.

The grant program supports large-scale projectsthat help address systemic racism, strengthen organizations, improve knowledge of racial unfairness, and create real, measurable change in Prince Edward Island.

Eligible projects must align with one or more of the following goals: 

  • Making changes to policies, practices, governance and organizational structures to remove barriers and address systemic racism 
  • Strengthening the ability of organizations and public institutions to advance anti-racism efforts
  • Empowering BIPOC communities by building partnerships, advocating for change and leading community-led research
  • Working to end systemic racism by bringing people together to take action and build community power 

  • Strengthening BIPOC community networks, leadership, and involvement in public life and decision-making

     

Projects may advance one or more of the following priority areas:

  • Reduce systemic racial barriers in institutions and services
  • Reform organizational governance and practices
  • Collect and analyze race-based data to better understand outcomes for different groups
  • Build organizational capacity to better support racialized and Indigenous communities
  • Address hate incidents and hate-related racism
  • Reduce harm against racialized and Indigenous women and gender-diverse people

Applications will be accepted until 11:59 p.m. on October 23, 2026. 

Quotes:

“We’re proud to invest in initiatives tackling systemic racism and creating lasting and meaningful change across PEI. By supporting these projects, we are empowering organizations to address barriers, strengthen communities, and make a positive difference in the lives of Islanders.”

-  Premier Rob Lantz

“The Anti-Racism Grant has been instrumental in helping Pride PEI develop the Common Cents Club and begin meaningful consultation with BIPOC community members and partners. Even in this early phase, we’re seeing excitement and interest in the project. We look forward to building on this momentum and moving into our next phase with purpose.”

-  Pride PEI executive director Cameron Cassidy

“The funding for the Bog Tours has been transformative. With more than 965 people taking the tour in 2026 alone, the response showed Islanders’ desire to learn about and connect with this largely untold history. The Bog has created a bridge between Black Islanders whose families have deep roots here and newer Black Islanders, connecting us through a shared heritage and strengthening a sense of belonging. Participants were often in awe to discover that Black people are not new to the Island; we were here before Confederation.” 

-  Black Cultural Society of PEI executive director Ujunwa Aja-Onu (Ujay)

To apply, and for more information about the grant, visit Anti-Racism Grants.

item.title: Premier McLeod on the Enbridge Line 21 Pipeline
item.description:
YELLOWKNIFE - Premier Bob McLeod issued the following statement on the Enbridge Line 21 pipeline today:

“I was pleased to learn that operations have resumed for Enbridge’s Line 21 pipeline after almost 2 years of no activity.

"Resource development has, and will continue to be, the backbone of our economy and is central to ensuring a good source of middle class jobs and business opportunities. Our territory has mineral and petroleum resources and the development of those resources can have a transformative effect on our people and economy.

"Sustainable economic development is key to the future of Northerners. With a strong resource development base, we will be able to support diversification of our local economies into emerging and established sectors.

"On behalf of the Government of the Northwest Territories I’d like to offer my congratulations to Imperial Oil, Enbridge the town of Norman Wells and other partners for getting this pipeline back up and running. I know the efforts and economic impacts of the pipeline have already begun to take shape in the community and will be felt for years to come. ”

 

Charlotte Digness
Media and Communications Coordinator
Cabinet Communications and Protocol
Government of the Northwest Territories
